szoveg_eredeti:
Transformer Artificial Intelligence Enables Scaled Analysis of Democratic Resilience Narratives

Democratic resilience relies as fundamentally on the shared civic narratives affirmed by a society as it does on formal legal and governing institutions. In recent decades, scholars across political science, sociology, and economics have documented how political narratives shape individual identities, mobilize collective social movements, and either sustain democratic governance or accelerate institutional breakdown. Quantifying how public discourse evolves has historically presented an intractable operational bottleneck for social scientists and policymakers. Investigating narrative framing traditionally demanded manual annotation by human domain experts, restricting empirical inquiry to modest textual corpora and slow collection cadences. Now, computational social science is experiencing a fundamental methodological pivot driven by transformer-based artificial intelligence architectures. By linking computational linguistics directly to established political theories of issue framing, researchers have demonstrated that modern neural language models can automate nuanced textual discrimination at massive scale, approaching and frequently exceeding the accuracy and consistency of trained human coders while reducing analytical costs by orders of magnitude.

The theoretical framework connecting democratic stability to computational narrative analysis operates across three distinct conceptual tiers. At the foundational level, democratic resilience is defined as a dynamic system capacity to withstand shocks such as extreme polarization while preserving essential governance functions, including electoral accountability, representative integrity, and constraints on concentrated executive power. Pernicious narratives directly undermine this resilience by eroding social trust, delegitimizing institutional checks, and promoting divisive political postures. In empirical applications, narratives are systematically operationalized through the lens of issue framing, defined as the selective emphasis of specific aspects of perceived reality to promote particular problem definitions, causal attributions, moral interpretations, or policy recommendations. Historically, rigorous framing research followed a six-step manual pipeline spanning issue identification, attitude isolation, frame definition, source selection, coding scheme validation, and manual document classification. Automated text-as-data methods seek to operationalize and accelerate this workflow, moving quantitative analysis from small sample sizes toward continuous, real-time observation of civic and legislative speech.

Understanding the transformative nature of modern natural language processing requires tracing the three historical waves of automated text analysis. The first technological wave relied on lexical token frequencies and bag-of-words representations, weighting terms through inverse document frequencies to construct numerical vectors. While computationally efficient, bag-of-words models stripped words of all grammatical and contextual syntax, unable to discern relational proximity between conceptually linked terms. The second wave introduced distributed semantic vector embeddings, using neural models such as Word2Vec to project vocabulary into shared geometric coordinate spaces based on contextual co-occurrence across extensive training corpora. Although semantic embeddings achieved marked improvements in word and document representation, they remained static and lacked the capacity to detect complex rhetorical devices such as irony, sarcasm, humor, or directional framing. Crucially, both earlier generations functioned purely as representational mechanisms rather than generative engines capable of contextual reasoning, semantic parsing, and adaptable conversational inquiry.

The advent of transformer architectures inaugurated a decisive third wave in natural language processing by fundamentally altering how neural models ingest, represent, and predict human language. Introduced through the attention mechanism, transformers process input text as unbroken sequential structures, utilizing positional encodings to preserve strict word order across arbitrarily long passages. Stacked encoder and decoder blocks employ multi-head self-attention mechanisms to simultaneously evaluate complex linguistic dependencies across entire sentences, tracking relations between verbs, pronouns, and nuanced modifiers. Optimized on massive web-scale corpora through self-supervised next-token prediction tasks, these architectures infer deep structural and semantic principles of communication. Autoregressive variants incorporate generated tokens back into input sequences, enabling generative language modeling that translates natural instructions into structured classifications. This underlying architecture allows large language models to display emergent analytical capabilities, mapping complex conceptual relationships, following granular analytical guidelines, and generalizing across specialized domains without task-specific architectural modification.

Across computational social science, transformers provide four distinct methodological functionalities that replace or augment traditional analytical workflows. First, encoder-only models such as BERT, RoBERTa, and Sentence-BERT serve as sophisticated representational drop-in replacements for traditional embedding vectors, boosting classifier accuracy when identifying specialized political framing in social media and legislative texts. Second, instruction-tuned generative models act as high-throughput automated labelers, achieving inter-rater reliability scores above ninety-five percent and matching or exceeding professional human annotator accuracy on political and moral classification tasks. Third, transformers function as synthetic data generators, producing tightly constrained, schema-compliant corpora that enable researchers to validate downstream classification pipelines in environments where genuine labeled records are costly or scarce. Fourth, modern generative models operate as direct framing analyzers, allowing researchers to measure textual alignment through probabilistic paired-completion experiments or uncover latent thematic structures across unannotated corpora using automated concept induction interfaces.

Deploying large language models for policy-relevant discourse analysis introduces critical methodological risks that demand rigorous experimental governance. Because these models are optimized via statistical next-token prediction, generated responses do not inherently guarantee empirical correctness, and models can stumble on subtle logical constraints. Commercial models are predominantly closed-source, raising issues surrounding computational cost, proprietary updates, and opaque training data provenance. Furthermore, empirical evaluations across political typology questionnaires reveal that major foundation models routinely exhibit structural left-of-centre ideological tendencies when deployed in unconstrained zero-shot settings. Human annotation in political science is itself vulnerable to partisan coder subjectivity, meaning machine evaluations trained on human feedback cannot be presumed completely neutral. Mitigating these systemic vulnerabilities requires strict prompt standardization, formal replication across multiple model architectures and research teams, explicit labeling definitions, and consistent calibration against expert-verified ground-truth benchmarks.

To evaluate the direct classification capabilities of transformer systems, researchers conducted an empirical trial assessing populist narratives across a benchmark corpus of five distinct political texts. The test corpus incorporated explicitly populist statements from Donald Trump, Belgium’s Vlaams Belang, and the French Left Front, alongside pro-democratic speeches from Barack Obama
